newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentines "black out" capital to protest austerity.
newsitem.headline: Argentines "black out" capital to protest austerity.

text.p: Argentines plunged their capital into darkness, banged their pots and honked their car horns on Thursday night to protest government austerity measures at a time of high unemployment.
The five-minute "blackout" organized by opposition parties appeared to draw widespread support among residents opposed to plans to increase taxes, cut family allowances and reduce worker benefits.
From the working class district of Floresta to the thriving community of Caballito, "portenos", as the capital's residents call themselves, turned out the lights.
The Radical Party and center-left Frepaso coalition joined forces for the first time for the protest that to them symbolized the government casting Argentines into darkness.
While the Peronist government of President Carlos Menem earlier dismissed the protest as "frivolous," the opposition was emboldened by the public's participation.
"This has been an impressive message. The people have had enough," Radical Party leader Rodolfo Terragno told reporters surrounded by a crush of supporters.

The ruling Peronist Party, seeking to reduce the effect of the protest, turned the lights on high outside key government offices, sent fireworks into the air and put on a laserlight display in the Plaza de Mayo across from the presidency.

But crowds supporting the protest gathered outside Congress and the central obelisk where earlier in the day the opposition released thousands of balloons into the sky, saying they symbolized "the frustrations of Argentines." Each balloon carried a promise made by Menem during seven years in power, such as a commitment a year ago to "pulverize unemployment."
Motorists honked their horns and pedestrians clapped their hands while others contributed to the cacophony by banging their kitchen pots on their balconies.
"It was a success," said Senator Graciela Fernandez Meijide of Frepaso. "The people clearly came out in favor of such a peaceful measure as this."
The private DyN news agency said residents of several other cities blacked out as well, while the state news agency Telam said adherence outside the capital was irregular.

After warnings from energy officials that the blackout and sudden surge of demand for power five minutes later could make the grid collapse, experts advised residents to unplug all domestic appliances and only turn them back on gradually. There were no immediate reports of energy problems.

"I can't see the sense of blackouts or strikes. They're not part of the solution, they're part of the problem," said Menem's chief of staff, Alberto Kohan. "A blackout doesn't solve anything, it shows impotence to come up with proposals."

The largest union federation, the CGT, refused to join in what it described was a "political" protest but vowed to stick to its 36-hour general strike in late September. Unions want measures to combat 17.1 percent unemployment.
The CGT was until recently an ally of Menem, and new CGT chief Rodolfo Daer said he was "disappointed" in the president he helped to return for a second term in May 1995 polls.

Daer, whose union held a strike last month, said Menem had overseen a "deep inequality among Argentines with businessmen, scientists, intellectuals, artists, workers and pensioners all living in a country where the future is uncertain."
